question: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

In its Special Report No 12/20261, the European Court of Auditors highlights serious shortcomings in the implementation of the European Union’s policies on artificial intelligence. In particular, it stresses the fragmented nature of initiatives, the lack of reliable performance indicators and persistent shortcomings in assessing the true impact of EU funding. This adds up to ineffectual governance of the issue and questionable use of public funds in what is, moreover, a field of the utmost strategic importance. The report also highlights the risks of overlap with national policies, revealing a worrying tendency to encroach upon the competences of Member States. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What specific measures it intends to take to ensure funding is no longer fragmented and truly effective?
On what grounds it justifies the proliferation of European initiatives in an area largely falling within the remit of national industrial strategies?
How it intends to comply with the principles of subsidiarity and sound financial management laid down in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union?
https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2026-12/SR-2026-12_EN.pdf.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) The Commission would like to note that the reference to 'serious shortcomings in the implementation of the EU’s policies on artificial intelligence’ does not appear in the Court of Auditor’s report1 mentioned in the written parliamentary question. Similarly, the report does not -in the context of AI policies- stress ’the fragmented nature of initiatives, the lack of reliable performance indicators and persistent shortcomings in assessing the true impact of EU funding’. The highlighted report is about the EU’s advisory bodies -notably the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions- and the impact of their opinions, not about the work of the Commission in a specific policy field. That said, the Commission would like to stress that, with regards to AI policies and initiatives, it has always closely coordinated its activities with those of Member States through existing discussion fora. For instance, when preparing the Apply AI Strategy2, the Commission based its work on the implementation of AI strategies and policy initiatives established by Member States. Direct contacts with Member States were made, including through interviews with key government entities responsible for the national AI strategies and policies, as well as through specific discussions in the AI Board. These contacts serve as a basis for understanding which practical gaps needed to be addressed and what coordinated approach to adopt in the Strategy. All these activities were organised in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity.
